strengths: Chorus provides a useful extension of scene-level 3DGS representation learning: a shared encoder distills language, general visual, and spatial features and supports multiple downstream tasks. Although the individual components are largely established, their integration and demonstrated transfer constitute a worthwhile computer vision contribution.

The empirical support is broad and includes substantial improvements. With the same listed training sources, Table 1 improves over SceneSplat from 21.4 to 24.6 foreground mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 10.1 to 15.7 on unseen InteriorGS. These results support both better semantic encoding and cross-dataset transfer.

The separately pretrained point-cloud-compatible variant is particularly interesting. Table 4 reports linear-probing improvements over Sonata from 28.8 to 36.0 mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 40.7 to 48.8 on ScanNet++. Improvements under full finetuning and across instance segmentation benchmarks provide evidence beyond a single evaluation protocol.

The teacher ablations support complementary supervision: in Table 9, adding DINO and then PE improves InteriorGS foreground mIoU from 8.0 to 9.3 to 11.4 for ScanNet++ pretraining. Figure 8 also provides useful evidence about augmentation and the timing of PE supervision.

Render-and-distill adaptation offers practical value. Table 7 reports a storage reduction from 1080 GB to 8 GB, while Figure 6 shows a 2.7-point linear-probing gain after adaptation on 100 scenes. Together with the broad transfer results, these supported benefits favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The most consequential ambiguity concerns supervision. Section 3.2 uses source-dataset semantic and instance labels for contrastive losses, and the implementation specifies nonzero contrastive weights, but the manuscript does not clearly identify their provenance and use for each experiment. This matters for interpreting zero-shot evaluation, comparisons with self-supervised Sonata, and especially Table 5: restricting downstream annotations does not establish low total annotation requirements if pretraining already uses fuller labels from those scenes.

The headline 8.32× and 39.9× efficiency claims measure training-scene counts, not matched information or computation. Chorus benefits from multiple large pretrained teachers, rendered views, and potentially label-based regularization. The reported comparisons demonstrate strong performance with fewer 3D scenes, but do not isolate an intrinsically more efficient learning algorithm. Table 7 also omits online teacher-inference cost and total adaptation time, so it establishes storage savings more clearly than faster adaptation.

The attribution of gains remains incomplete. The method builds on SceneSplat-style lifting, a Sonata-derived backbone, established multi-teacher projectors, and PHI-S. Table 9 isolates incremental teachers for semantic segmentation, but does not establish PE's contribution to instance segmentation or reasoning. Likewise, Table 8 compares differently pretrained encoders; it cannot isolate Gaussian pretraining as the cause of noise robustness without a point-cloud-pretrained control using the same teachers and objectives.

Reproducibility is limited in the supplied manuscript. Important details are deferred to an unavailable supplement, including augmentation equations and additional training settings. The new InteriorGS benchmark lacks an explicit split and per-Gaussian label-construction protocol, and the precise supervision restrictions for data-efficient experiments are unspecified. These omissions affect reconstruction of the experimental comparisons, beyond presentation quality.

Several claims should be narrowed to match the tables. Chorus trails Sonata on ScanNet instance probing and several limited-data probing settings; ScanQA METEOR also decreases from 22.9 to 22.5. Smaller ablation gains lack uncertainty estimates. Minor reporting errors include ScanNet++ finetuning described as 50.2 mIoU versus 52.9 in Table 4, and the Table 5 semantic-segmentation improvement described as mAP.

strengths: Chorus addresses a useful problem: learning transferable, feed-forward features directly from Gaussian scene representations. The combination of complementary teachers, shared encoding, and teacher-specific projectors is technically coherent, although its novelty is primarily in integration and application.

The empirical support is substantial. With matched source datasets, Table 1 improves over SceneSplat from 21.4 to 24.6 foreground mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 10.1 to 15.7 on the unseen InteriorGS dataset. These results support improved semantic representation and cross-dataset transfer.

Evaluation extends meaningfully beyond open-vocabulary segmentation. Table 4 reports strong point-cloud transfer, including linear-probing gains over Sonata of 7.2 mIoU on ScanNet200 and 8.1 on ScanNet++. Instance segmentation, limited-supervision experiments, and backbone replacement within GaussianVLM provide additional evidence of usefulness.

The ablations substantiate parts of the design: Table 9 shows gains from adding DINO and further cross-domain gains from PE; Figure 8 supports staged teacher introduction. Rendering-based adaptation also offers a practical storage advantage and improves InteriorGS linear probing by 2.7 mIoU. Taken together, these supported contributions favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The supervision protocol needs substantially clearer accounting. Section 3.2 uses semantic and instance labels for contrastive regularization, and the implementation specifies nonzero contrastive weights, but the manuscript does not identify precisely which datasets and experiments use these labels or whether they are ground truth or pseudo-labels. This matters directly for interpreting zero-shot evaluation and limited-annotation results: downstream annotation restrictions do not establish overall label efficiency if richer annotations were already used during pretraining. This is an unresolved protocol ambiguity, not evidence of test-set leakage.

The headline 8.32× and 39.9× data-efficiency claims count 3D training scenes without controlling teacher supervision, dataset composition, annotation availability, or computation. They demonstrate fewer task-specific pretraining scenes, but do not establish equivalent-resource efficiency against self-supervised Sonata. Table 7 also reports rasterization overhead without quantifying the full cost of online teacher inference and adaptation training.

The evidence does not fully isolate the source of the gains. Chorus changes teachers, objectives, augmentations, and model capacity relative to SceneSplat. Table 9 provides useful semantic-segmentation ablations, but does not directly establish that PE improves instance grouping or that multi-teacher learning drives the VQA gains. Likewise, Table 8's noise-retrieval comparison cannot isolate Gaussian-based pretraining as the cause of robustness without a matched point-cloud-trained distillation control.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Important details are deferred to a supplement that is not included: augmentation equations and strengths, substantial pretraining settings, and contrastive-loss details. The proposed InteriorGS benchmark also lacks a sufficiently explicit split and label-construction protocol. Small ablation gains are reported without variation across runs.

Some claims exceed the reported results. Chorus underperforms Sonata on ScanNet instance probing and several limited-data probing settings, while ScanQA METEOR decreases from 22.9 to 22.5. Table 2 uses external Mask3D proposals, so it primarily supports better instance recognition rather than independently learned instance discovery. Correctable reporting issues include the ScanNet++ finetuning discrepancy between the text (50.2) and Table 4 (52.9), and describing a semantic-segmentation improvement as mAP.

strengths: Chorus makes a useful empirical contribution to transferable 3D Gaussian scene representations. Combining language-aligned, generalist, and spatial teachers through a shared encoder is technically coherent, and the extensive downstream evaluation provides a stronger acceptance case than the novelty of any individual component.

The semantic segmentation gains are substantial across multiple datasets. With the same listed training sources, Chorus improves over SceneSplat from 21.4 to 24.6 foreground mIoU on ScanNet200, 13.8 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, and 10.1 to 15.7 on the unseen InteriorGS domain (Table 1). These results support both representation quality and cross-domain usefulness.

The separately pretrained point-cloud-compatible variant demonstrates valuable transfer. Linear probing improves over Sonata from 28.8 to 36.0 mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 40.7 to 48.8 on ScanNet++; full finetuning also improves across all five reported semantic benchmarks (Table 4). Table 5 additionally shows consistent advantages under limited supervision when fully finetuned.

Evidence extends beyond semantic segmentation. With common Mask3D proposals, Chorus improves open-vocabulary instance mAP50 from 16.0 to 18.0 over Mosaic3D and tail-class performance from 5.4 to 13.0 (Table 2). Replacing the GaussianVLM encoder also improves several question-answering metrics, supporting broader utility.

The teacher ablations provide concrete evidence of complementarity: on InteriorGS, adding DINO and then PE increases foreground mIoU from 8.0 to 9.3 to 11.4 for ScanNet++ pretraining (Table 9). Rendering-based adaptation is also practically promising, with a reported 2.7-point linear-probing gain using 100 additional scenes and greatly reduced feature storage.
weaknesses: The supervision protocol is insufficiently explicit for interpreting the zero-shot and annotation-efficiency claims. Section 3.2 uses source semantic and instance labels for contrastive regularization, and the implementation specifies nonzero contrastive weights, but the manuscript does not clearly identify which datasets and reported checkpoints use these labels. In particular, Table 5 does not establish whether pretraining used annotations beyond its downstream label budgets. This does not demonstrate test leakage, but it materially limits comparisons with self-supervised Sonata and the interpretation of annotation efficiency.

The methodological novelty is primarily an integration of established components: SceneSplat-style lifting, a Sonata-derived encoder, existing multi-teacher distillation and PHI-S normalization, and conventional matching and contrastive losses. Teacher ablations focus on semantic segmentation; corresponding controlled instance and VQA ablations would be needed to substantiate the stronger explanation that teacher complementarity specifically produces holistic capabilities. The noisy-point retrieval experiment likewise does not isolate Gaussian pretraining from the different supervision objectives.

The 8.32× and 39.9× efficiency claims concern counts of 3D training scenes, rather than matched supervision or computational resources. Chorus benefits from three large pretrained image teachers and potentially source labels. Table 7 establishes storage and preprocessing savings for adaptation, but reports rasterization overhead without total online teacher inference and training time. Consequently, broad computational-efficiency or faster-adaptation claims are not fully established.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details in the supplied manuscript. These include the pretraining schedule and optimizer settings, matching-loss coefficients, precise augmentation definitions, and sufficient information about the new InteriorGS benchmark's splits and label handling. Several essential details are deferred to a supplement absent from the provided PDF; promised future code does not resolve these omissions.

Some claims need narrower wording, and several reporting issues are readily correctable. Chorus trails Sonata on ScanNet instance probing and on several limited-data probing settings; ScanQA METEOR decreases from 22.9 to 22.5. Thus, performance is strong but not uniformly superior. The text also reports ScanNet++ finetuning as 50.2 mIoU whereas Table 4 gives 52.9, and describes the Table 5 semantic gain as mAP. No variability estimates are provided for the smaller improvements.

strengths: Chorus makes a useful contribution to transferable 3DGS representation learning. Combining complementary 2D teachers through a shared encoder and separate projectors is technically coherent, and the work extends SceneSplat beyond language-aligned semantic features to a substantially broader set of tasks.

The strongest evidence is the breadth and magnitude of segmentation improvements. In Table 1, joint-training foreground mIoU improves over SceneSplat from 22.5 to 24.6 on ScanNet200, 14.0 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, and 10.0 to 15.7 on unseen InteriorGS. Retraining SceneSplat on the updated data helps make this comparison credible.

Transfer to point-cloud benchmarks is compelling. Table 4 reports linear-probing gains over Sonata of 7.2 mIoU on ScanNet200 and 8.1 on ScanNet++, with substantial gains retained after finetuning. Instance segmentation and sparse-label experiments provide additional evidence that the representation is useful beyond one evaluation protocol.

The ablations substantiate several design choices. Table 9 and supplementary Table C demonstrate benefits from combining language and DINO supervision; Figure 8 supports staged PE supervision and 3DGS-aware augmentation. Tests across Gaussian optimization methods, density reductions, and iPhone captures further strengthen the practical evidence.

Render-and-distill adaptation offers a useful storage tradeoff: Table 7 reports reducing stored preprocessing outputs from 1080 GB to 8 GB, while Figure 6 shows a 2.7 mIoU improvement after adaptation on 100 InteriorGS scenes. Overall, the supported empirical contribution favors acceptance despite the qualifications below.
weaknesses: The supervision budget is insufficiently disentangled. Section 3.2 explicitly uses semantic and instance labels for contrastive regularization, and the implementation enables these terms, but the manuscript does not clearly enumerate their use across datasets and reported models. Consequently, comparisons against self-supervised Sonata, especially limited-annotation experiments, do not establish equivalent total annotation budgets. The 39.9× and 8.32× figures measure scene counts, not equivalent supervision or compute; they should not be interpreted as general efficiency advantages.

The central multi-teacher contribution is supported more directly for semantics than for holistic capability. Teacher ablations primarily evaluate semantic segmentation; there are no corresponding teacher-removal results for instance segmentation or VQA. Moreover, adding PE lowers InteriorGS decoder-probing mIoU from 28.9 to 28.3 in Table C. Open-vocabulary instance evaluation uses fixed Mask3D proposals, so its gains establish better proposal recognition rather than improved instance discovery. The evidence supports useful complementary features, but not uniformly improved instance grouping.

The explanation that Gaussian pretraining itself induces point-cloud robustness is not isolated experimentally. Table 8 compares encoders differing in objectives and supervision as well as training representation. A matched multi-teacher model pretrained directly on point clouds is absent. The retrieval results establish robustness of Chorus, but do not identify Gaussian inputs as its cause.

Adaptation claims need qualification. Supplementary Section A.2 uses semantic labels to choose camera heights and supplied occupancy maps to sample positions; the demonstrated pipeline therefore requires more than rendered frames alone. Table 7 reports rasterization overhead but does not quantify complete adaptation time including online teacher inference. The storage benefit is clear, whereas the claimed acceleration is less firmly established.

InteriorGS evaluation relies on heuristic per-Gaussian labels derived from bounding boxes and largest connected components. No quantitative annotation audit is provided, and resolving overlapping component assignments is underspecified. This limits confidence in the precise benchmark scores, although the independent ScanNet-family results substantially mitigate this concern.

Reproducibility and presentation have remaining gaps. The supplement provides useful processing details but does not fully specify the main pretraining optimizer, schedule, batch size, loss coefficients, or normal estimation. Small gains lack repeated-run uncertainty. Several statements also overreach the tables: ScanQA METEOR decreases, ScanNet instance probing trails Sonata, and the text reports ScanNet++ finetuning as 50.2 mIoU whereas Table 4 gives 52.9. These reporting issues are secondary to the methodological qualifications above.

strengths: The supported empirical contribution favors weak acceptance. Chorus provides a useful feed-forward representation for both Gaussian scenes and point clouds, with improvements across multiple established benchmarks. The contribution is primarily a well-tested integration of existing techniques rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation improves over the directly relevant SceneSplat baseline across all four joint-training evaluations in Table 1: foreground mIoU increases from 22.5 to 24.6 on ScanNet200, 14.0 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, 28.6 to 29.6 on ScanNet++, and 10.0 to 15.7 on held-out InteriorGS. Retraining SceneSplat on the updated data strengthens this comparison.

Transfer evaluation is unusually broad. Table 4 shows substantial linear-probing gains over Sonata on ScanNet200 (36.0 versus 28.8 mIoU) and ScanNet++ (48.8 versus 40.7), alongside strong full-finetuning results. Instance segmentation, limited-annotation experiments, and language-model integration provide additional evidence of practical usefulness.

The teacher ablations offer direct evidence that combining signals helps: Table 9 improves upon language-only supervision, while supplementary Table C compares against DINO-only and language-only alternatives. Figure 8 additionally examines loss choice, augmentation, teacher staging, and instance contrastive supervision.

Rendering-based adaptation addresses a practical storage bottleneck. Table 7 reports reducing stored preprocessing data from 1080 GB to 8 GB, and Figure 6 reports a 2.7-point linear-probing improvement with 100 adaptation scenes. Tests across Gaussian optimization methods, densities, and iPhone captures further support robustness.
weaknesses: The supervision budget is insufficiently specified. Section 3.2 and supplementary Section A.1 explicitly permit semantic and instance labels in pretraining contrastive losses, but the experiments do not clearly identify which annotations are used for each checkpoint. This matters particularly for the zero-shot and limited-annotation claims: if pretraining already uses extensive target-dataset annotations, Table 5 measures restricted downstream supervision rather than overall annotation efficiency. The manuscript does not establish that leakage occurred, but it leaves this consequential protocol question unresolved.

The headline 8.32× and 39.9× efficiency claims measure scene counts, not equivalent supervision or computation. Chorus benefits from several large pretrained image teachers, multi-view images, Gaussian reconstruction, and offline feature lifting; Sonata uses a different learning regime. These results support economical use of 3D scenes, but do not establish comparable total training efficiency. End-to-end adaptation timing also omits a clear accounting of online teacher inference.

The attribution of gains to Gaussian pretraining remains incomplete. The noise-retrieval comparison in Table 8 changes both representation and training objective; it cannot isolate the claim that Gaussian inputs themselves act as beneficial augmentation. A matched multi-teacher point-cloud pretraining control is absent. Teacher ablations mainly assess semantic segmentation, leaving the claimed object-aware contribution to instance grouping less directly tested.

The adaptation pipeline has prerequisites understated by the main text. Supplementary Section A.2 uses supplied occupancy maps and semantic labels to select camera heights. Thus, the demonstrated procedure is not established for arbitrary unlabeled Gaussian scenes. InteriorGS evaluation also relies on bounding-box-derived labels assigned using a largest-connected-component heuristic, without a quantitative annotation-quality audit or a clear rule for residual overlapping assignments.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful supplementary details. The main pretraining schedule, optimizer settings, batch size, contrastive warm-up duration, and several augmentation hyperparameters are not fully specified. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, which limits interpretation of small incremental gains such as those from adding PE-Spatial.

Several claims need narrower wording. Chorus trails Sonata on ScanNet instance linear probing and some decoder-probing settings; adding PE reduces decoder mIoU from 28.9 to 28.3 in supplementary Table C. ScanQA METEOR also decreases. Moreover, the VQA experiment changes the connector to a single attention block, so performance and speed differences cannot be attributed solely to the encoder. These qualifications weaken claims of uniformly superior performance, while leaving the broader empirical contribution intact.

strengths: Chorus makes a useful empirical contribution to general-purpose 3DGS representation learning. Although its components build on existing methods, combining complementary teachers in a shared scene encoder delivers sufficiently broad and substantial benefits to support weak acceptance.

Semantic results are strong across multiple datasets. Against the retrained SceneSplat baseline, joint pretraining improves foreground mIoU from 22.5 to 24.6 on ScanNet200, 14.0 to 18.7 on Matterport3D, and 10.0 to 15.7 on InteriorGS (Table 1). The InteriorGS result is particularly valuable because this dataset is excluded from pretraining.

The point-cloud-compatible variant demonstrates meaningful transfer beyond native Gaussian inputs. Linear probing improves over Sonata from 28.8 to 36.0 mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 40.7 to 48.8 on ScanNet++; full finetuning also produces substantial gains (Table 4). The evaluation includes instance segmentation and limited-annotation settings, providing evidence beyond a single benchmark.

Teacher ablations support complementarity: adding DINO improves language-only pretraining, and adding PE further improves zero-shot transfer to InteriorGS (Table 9). Tests with alternative Gaussian optimization, reduced Gaussian density, and iPhone point clouds provide useful robustness evidence.

Rendering-based adaptation offers a practical storage tradeoff and measurable transfer gains: approximately 2.7 mIoU improvement with 100 adaptation scenes, alongside substantially reduced cached-feature storage (Figure 6 and Table 7). The supplement provides useful implementation details, teacher specifications, data processing procedures, and benchmark splits.
weaknesses: The supervision accounting is insufficiently explicit for the zero-shot and data-efficiency claims. Sections 3.2 and A.1 use semantic and instance labels for contrastive grouping, and the main implementation enables contrastive losses, but the manuscript does not clearly enumerate which annotations are used in each reported model. This matters especially when comparing against self-supervised Sonata or evaluating limited downstream annotations. The 8.32× and 39.9× ratios describe 3D scene counts, not matched annotation, teacher-pretraining, or computational budgets.

The methodological novelty is primarily an integration of established components: SceneSplat-style lifting, a Sonata-derived backbone, teacher-specific projectors, PHI-S normalization, and standard matching/contrastive losses. Ablations support semantic benefits, but do not directly establish that PE improves learned instance grouping or that multi-teacher training drives the VQA gains. Table 2 uses external Mask3D proposals, and Table C actually shows lower decoder-probing mIoU after adding PE (28.9 to 28.3).

The adaptation pipeline has stronger prerequisites than the main description suggests. Supplement A.2 uses InteriorGS occupancy maps and semantic labels to choose camera heights, so the demonstrated procedure is not solely based on unlabeled rendered frames. Table 7 reports rasterization overhead but not the complete recurring teacher-inference and optimization cost, limiting the evidence for faster or lightweight adaptation.

The proposed InteriorGS benchmark derives per-Gaussian labels through bounding-box membership and largest connected components, without a reported manual accuracy audit or sensitivity analysis. This heuristic can retain touching background geometry or discard disconnected object parts; handling overlapping assignments is also underspecified. Consequently, absolute semantic and instance accuracy on this new benchmark is less firmly established than on the existing datasets.

Some claims and reproducibility details need qualification. Chorus trails Sonata on ScanNet instance linear probing and several low-data probing settings, while ScanQA METEOR decreases despite the claim of consistent improvements. Section 4.2 reports ScanNet++ finetuning as 50.2 mIoU, whereas Table 4 gives 52.9. The VQA connector also changes according to Supplement C.2, complicating backbone-only attribution. Core pretraining schedules and augmentation magnitudes are not fully specified, and repeated-run uncertainty is absent for small gains. These issues temper the recommendation but do not outweigh the larger, broadly supported improvements.
